reasons.C1: Secret price-fixing offers to pricing agents is a sensible, moderately novel framing; say-versus-do split adds value.
reasons.C2: Careful design, preregistration and tests, but zero real model runs; no results to judge, only a mock pipeline.
reasons.C3: Design is described clearly, but there are no findings and no report; core content of a research write-up is missing.

levers.C1: Show that acceptance rates differ sharply across offer framings and model families, revealing a measurable susceptibility no one has quantified.
levers.C2: Run the 60 games on real models, pass the positive control, and report accept and price rates with Wilson intervals.
levers.C3: Deliver the 8-page report with a results table per condition, the positive control first, and explicit limitations.

R6.verdict: Solid preregistered skeleton, but without a single real run it is a protocol, not a result.

reasons.C1: Real on-chain detection of self-funded buyers is useful for assurance, but wallets are not shown to be AI agents.
reasons.C2: Held-out split, permutation and bootstrap are good; ten test families, wide interval and label leakage weaken the 0.82.
reasons.C3: Claims and numbers are interpretable, but the 17-page report exceeds the 8-page limit and dilutes focus.

levers.C1: Link flagged wallets to verified LLM agents and show the rule catches coordination that existing wash-trading detectors miss.
levers.C2: Use independent labels without shared evidence and many more held-out families, keeping the feature-disjoint result significant.
levers.C3: Cut to 8 pages with one headline table: held-out accuracy, feature-disjoint control, spot-check, and the named blind spots.

V4.verdict: Honest, real-data forensics with decent statistics, but it detects wallet rings, not demonstrated AI collusion.

reasons.C1: Testing whether leniency and fines act on LLM sellers as on humans is policy-relevant and neglected; benchmarked against published human data.
reasons.C2: No code or data; the plan with contamination test and preregistration is rigorous but entirely unevidenced.
reasons.C3: Plan, controls, cut order and demo table are stated clearly; nothing exists yet to present as findings.

levers.C1: Show a regime where LLM agents diverge from humans, for example leniency backfiring, with a mechanism others can test.
levers.C2: Pass the paper-table tests, run the pilot positive control, and deliver all four regimes with intervals and contamination checks.
levers.C3: Produce the promised human-versus-LLM scorecard table with intervals as the report's first figure.

K8.verdict: The most policy-relevant question here, but it is still a plan; ambitious for 48 solo hours.

reasons.C1: Latent vector channels evading text monitors matter for oversight, but channels are non-adaptive and no collusion game is tested.
reasons.C2: Real models, reproduce log 10 of 10, shuffled-label probe control, text baseline; few seeds, no significance tests.
reasons.C3: Figure 1 makes the key result obvious; report and controls are clear, though 13 pages exceeds the limit.

levers.C1: Train channels adaptively against snapping and probes inside an actual collusion task, showing whether the countermeasure survives an adversary.
levers.C2: Add adversarially trained channels, more seeds with significance tests, and publish checkpoints so results are independently verifiable.
levers.C3: Trim to 8 pages and state upfront which work was done before the sprint versus during it.

K3.verdict: Best-validated entry: a clean, reproducible negative result for latent channels, limited by non-adaptive attackers and no collusion setting.
